946.title: Tashlich, casting away
946.hook: Jews cast crumbs into flowing water, symbolizing sins cast away (Micah 7:19)
946.howItsDone: On the afternoon of Rosh Hashanah, some Jews go to a river, stream or sea to recite verses from Micah and the Psalms; some toss bread crumbs onto the water, and some shake out their pockets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yamim Noraim, from the new year to the Day of Atonement. Your line was ten days. Did you cross a name off your list? Today, one small thing Jews do inside those days, at the water's edge. Day nine hundred forty-six.

An afternoon by a river. People in good clothes, the kind you'd wear to synagogue, are standing along the bank. Some hold small prayer books. A grandfather lifts a child so she can see over the rail. Someone takes a few crumbs of bread from a pocket and tosses them onto the water, and the current carries them off downstream. A woman simply turns her coat pockets inside out and shakes them over the edge. Nobody is feeding the ducks, exactly. They're acting out a line from one of the prophets, about where wrongs go.
screen: `AN AFTERNOON BY A RIVER.` → `CRUMBS ON THE CURRENT.` → `A LINE FROM A PROPHET.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. The prophet Micah ends his book with a question and a promise. In the King James words: "Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy." And then: "He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea." Second, the name. In Micah's Hebrew, the word for thou wilt cast gives the custom its name: tashlich. On Rosh Hashanah, in the afternoon, Jews in some places walk to flowing water, a river, a stream, the sea, and say verses from Micah and the Psalms. Some toss crumbs. Some just shake out their pockets. Third, what the crumbs are. The bread doesn't carry the sins away by itself. In the tradition's own telling, the turning back, the teshuvah, is the work. The crumbs are a picture of it, something for the hands to do. You see the thing leave. You watch it go where you can't reach it anymore. Fourth, the end of a stretch. With tashlich we close the Jewish voices on forgiveness. Teshuvah, the return. Four steps. Ask them first. Joseph weeping. Esau running. Ten days. And now the river. It's worth noticing who does the casting in Micah's verse. Not the person. God casts the sins into the depths, and the depths, by the verse's own picture, are a place nobody goes to fish them back out.
screen: `HE DELIGHTETH IN MERCY.` · `THOU WILT CAST: TASHLICH.` · `THE CRUMBS ARE A PICTURE.` · `INTO THE DEPTHS OF THE SEA.` · then, large: `CAST IT AWAY.`

segments.voice: If there's water near you, a stream, a fountain, even a bowl of water on the table, find a leaf or a small scrap and bring it close. If there isn't, close your eyes and see one. Sit with it, and breathe. Let one thing you're ready to put down come to mind: a resentment, a regret, an old wrong you've already turned from. Give it to the leaf. Then let the leaf drop onto the water, or let it go in your mind, and watch it drift. Don't reach for it. If you pray, you can say a line from Micah. The bell holds the time.
Tashlich. Hebrew, from Micah's thou wilt cast: the custom on Rosh Hashanah of going to flowing water and casting crumbs, a picture of wrongs cast away. Today's word.
Your line: cast it away. Today, when the thing you dropped floats back up, see the leaf again, drifting downstream, and leave it there. Day nine hundred forty-six.

947.title: As we forgive
947.hook: forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors (Matthew 6:12)
947.howItsDone: Christians pray the Lord's Prayer in private and together in church; depending on the church and the translation, the line says debts, sins or trespasses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tashlich: crumbs on moving water, and the line from Micah about sins cast into the depths of the sea. Your line was cast it away. What did you let the river take? Today, the Christian voices begin, with one small word in a famous prayer. Day nine hundred forty-seven.

A stadium before a game. A hospital chapel at night. A classroom, a wedding, a funeral. Somewhere, right now, people are saying the Lord's Prayer together, some fast and some slow, a few half a beat behind. And in the middle of it comes a line people say so smoothly they can sail right past it. Forgive us, as we forgive. Two words sit in that line like a hinge: as we. The person praying asks for mercy, and in the same breath ties that mercy to their own. Today: as we forgive.
screen: `SAID IN STADIUMS AND CHAPELS.` → `A LINE THAT GOES BY FAST.` → `TWO WORDS LIKE A HINGE.`

segments.voice: Start with the words Jesus taught, in Matthew's Gospel. The King James has it this way: "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Debts. Not feelings, not moods. The picture is a ledger. Somebody owes, and forgiving means tearing up what's owed. That's the first turn: in this prayer, a wrong is something like a bill, and mercy is letting the bill go unpaid. Second, the other versions. Luke's Gospel gives the same prayer a little differently: "forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us." And the Book of Common Prayer, the prayer book of the Church of England, says trespasses: "forgive us our trespasses, As we forgive them that trespass against us." Debts, sins, trespasses. Churches still say it different ways, and each word lights a different corner of the same room. Third, the hinge. Right after the prayer, Matthew has Jesus come back to one line, and only one: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." Of all the lines in the prayer, this is the one the text stops to underline. Christians read it in more than one way. Some hear a condition: mercy received and mercy given come as a pair. Others hear a description: a heart that has really taken in forgiveness starts to give it away, the way a full cup spills. Christian teachers have argued over that balance, and the prayer holds it without settling it for anyone. Fourth, the plain fact of saying it. Each time someone prays this line, they name their own debts and their debtors in one sentence. You can't say it without remembering that somebody owes you something too. For anyone, praying or not, that's a useful mirror: what am I asking to be let off, and what am I still holding over someone else?
screen: `DEBTS: A WRONG AS A BILL.` · `DEBTS, SINS, TRESPASSES.` · `THE ONE LINE THE TEXT UNDERLINES.` · `A MIRROR: WHAT DO I HOLD?` · then, large: `AS WE FORGIVE OUR DEBTORS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind one small debt someone owes you. Not the deepest wound. Something modest: a borrowed book, an apology that never came, a favor that wasn't returned. See the ledger in your mind, with their name and the amount. Now, just for this sit, picture tearing up that one line. Not because it didn't matter, but because you choose to stop collecting. Notice what happens in your chest when you do. If you pray, you can say the line from the Lord's Prayer slowly, with that person in mind. The bell holds the time.
Trespasses. One Christian version's word for the wrongs forgiven in the Lord's Prayer, debts in Matthew, sins in Luke. Today's word.
Your line: a full cup spills. Today, forgive one small debt for real: stop waiting for the book, the favor or the apology, and don't mention it again. Day nine hundred forty-seven.

948.title: Seventy times seven
948.hook: Peter asks: seven times? Jesus: seventy times seven (Matthew 18:21–22)
948.carry: a number too big to keep track of
948.howItsDone: Christian teachers turn to Matthew 18:21–22 when speaking about forgiveness in families and congregations, and preachers sometimes pair it with the verses just before it on going to the person who wronged you.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trespasses, the hinge in the Lord's Prayer. Your line was a full cup spills. Which small debt did you stop collecting? Today, a disciple asks how many times that has to happen. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

How many times is enough? Ask it about the roommate who leaves the dishes, again, or the coworker who takes credit in the meeting, says sorry after, and does it the next week. The first time, letting it go feels generous. The third time it feels foolish. Somewhere around there, a reasonable person starts asking where the line is. Peter, one of Jesus's closest followers, asked exactly that, out loud, and even offered a number that sounds generous. Today: seventy times seven.
screen: `AGAIN. AND AGAIN.` → `WHERE'S THE LINE?` → `PETER OFFERS A NUMBER.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Matthew tells it in two short verses. In the King James words, Peter asks: "Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?" Notice the shape. It isn't a stranger. It's my brother, someone close, someone who will keep showing up. And Peter's number isn't stingy. Seven times is a lot of patience with one person. Second, the answer. Jesus says: "I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." Some readers take the Greek as seventy times seven, others as seventy-seven times. Either way, the point isn't a bigger number to count up to. It's a number too big to keep track of. If you're tallying to seventy-seven, you've missed the point. The answer quietly takes the counting away. Third, a companion line. Luke's Gospel has a version of this teaching that is even more domestic: "if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him." Seven times in one day. That's not a betrayal once a decade. That's ordinary life, with someone you live alongside. Fourth, what it doesn't say. The answer doesn't tell Peter to pretend nothing happened, or to stop telling his brother the truth. In Matthew, the verses just before this one lay out how to go to a brother who has wronged you and speak to him directly. Some Christian teachers read the two together: you can name the wrong, set a limit, even keep your distance, and still refuse to keep a running total in your heart. Forgiveness, in this reading, is about the count kept inside, not about letting harm continue.
screen: `HOW OFT? TILL SEVEN TIMES?` · `A NUMBER TOO BIG TO COUNT.` · `SEVEN TIMES IN A DAY.` · `NAME IT, BUT STOP THE TALLY.` · then, large: `UNTIL SEVENTY TIMES SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Picture one thing someone close to you does again and again. Not something dangerous, just something that wears on you. Notice the little counter in your head: that's the fifth time, the tenth time. For these two minutes, try setting the counter down. You can still think it's wrong. You can still plan to talk about it. Just let the number go. Each time the tally comes back, and it will, breathe out and set it down again. If you pray, you can name that person once more, without a number attached. The bell holds the time.
Peter. The disciple who asked Jesus how often to forgive, and got an answer too big to keep count. Today's word.
Your line: a number too big to keep track of. Today, forgive the same small thing again, the one you're tired of forgiving, and notice whether you're still counting. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

949.title: The unforgiving servant
949.hook: a man forgiven a huge debt throttles someone over a small one (Matthew 18:23–35)
949.howItsDone: Christians read the parable of the unforgiving servant as part of Jesus's answer to Peter about forgiveness, since Matthew places it right after seventy times seven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter's question and the answer that took the counting away. Your line was a number too big to keep track of. Did you catch the tally starting up again? Today, the story Jesus tells right after that answer. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

A king sits down to go through his accounts, and one servant is brought in owing him ten thousand talents. The text says plainly he has nothing to pay it with. The king orders him sold, with his wife and children and everything he has. The servant falls down before him and begs: be patient, I'll pay it all. And the king, moved with compassion, lets him go and forgives the whole debt. The servant walks out a free man. Then he goes out, and what he does next is the whole story. Today: the unforgiving servant.
screen: `TEN THOUSAND TALENTS.` → `BE PATIENT, I'LL PAY IT ALL.` → `THE WHOLE DEBT, FORGIVEN.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. Outside, the forgiven servant runs into a fellow servant who owes him an hundred pence, in the King James words. A small sum, set right beside an impossible one. And the text says he "laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest." The fellow servant falls down and begs with almost the same words: "Have patience with me, and I will pay thee all." The same plea that just saved the first man. He refuses, and has him thrown in prison until he pays. Second, the witnesses. The other servants see it, and they're very sorry, and they go and tell the king everything. The story doesn't let this happen in private. Mercy, and the lack of it, gets noticed. Third, the question at the center. The king calls the man back and asks: "Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?" Even as I had pity on thee. That's the whole parable in one line. The servant's problem isn't that he wanted his money. It's that he walked out of the biggest mercy of his life and didn't let it change a single thing about how he treated anyone else. Fourth, the hard ending. The king hands him over to the tormentors, and Jesus closes with a warning about forgiving a brother from the heart. Christians read that ending differently. Some take it as a stark warning about judgment. Others hear it as a picture of what an unforgiving heart already does to itself: it locks itself in. Both readings keep the same center. The man forgot he had been forgiven.
screen: `BY THE THROAT, OVER A SMALL DEBT.` · `THE OTHER SERVANTS SEE IT.` · `EVEN AS I HAD PITY ON THEE.` · `A HARD ENDING, READ TWO WAYS.` · then, large: `SHOULDEST NOT THOU ALSO HAVE HAD COMPASSION?`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind a time someone let you off. A parent who didn't stay angry. A friend who took you back. A teacher who gave a second chance, a boss who let a mistake go, a stranger who was kind when you'd been rude. Stay with that memory for a minute. What did you owe them? What did they choose not to collect? Then, gently, let someone come to mind who owes you something small today. Hold the two side by side, the way the story does. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's words for the mercy you received. The bell holds the time.
Talents. The enormous debt, ten thousand of them, that a king forgave a servant who then seized a fellow servant over a small one. Today's word.
Your line: I was forgiven too. Today, the next time someone's small debt gets under your skin, remember one time you were let off, before you say anything. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

950.title: Father, forgive them
950.hook: from the cross: they know not what they do (Luke 23:34)
950.howItsDone: Christians remember this line among the sayings of Jesus from the cross, read especially on Good Friday, and some churches meditate on the sayings one by one that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man forgiven everything who seized someone over a small debt. Your line was I was forgiven too. Which mercy did you remember? Today, forgiveness spoken at the worst possible moment. Day nine hundred fifty.

Luke's Gospel slows down at the place called Calvary. Two criminals, one on each side. A crowd standing and watching. And in that moment, before the soldiers cast lots for his clothes and the mocking that follows, Luke records a sentence from Jesus. It isn't a cry of pain. It isn't a curse. It's addressed upward, and it's about the people right in front of him. Today: Father, forgive them.
screen: `A PLACE CALLED CALVARY.` → `TWO CRIMINALS, ONE ON EACH SIDE.` → `A SENTENCE ADDRESSED UPWARD.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. In the King James: "Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Notice the first word. Father. It's the same word that opens the prayer Jesus teaches in Luke, and he says it here, too, of all places. Not judge, not avenger. The family word, spoken from the worst day. Second, who he forgives. The sentence doesn't name names, and Christians have read it in different ways. Some hear it about the soldiers carrying out orders. Some widen it to everyone who had a hand in it. Others widen it further still, to every person, themselves included. The text leaves the circle open, and that openness is part of its force. Third, the reason he gives. For they know not what they do. That's a striking thing to say about people carrying out a crucifixion. Some readers point out that they know what their hands are doing; what they don't see, in this reading, is what it means: who this is, what it costs, what they've become part of. Read that way, the line holds two truths at once. A wrong is happening. And the people doing it don't fully understand it. Forgiveness here doesn't pretend the first truth away. It leans on the second. Fourth, what this does for ordinary life. Sometimes the people who hurt us aren't villains with a plan. They're tired, scared, careless, following orders, repeating what was done to them. They know what they did. They may not see all of what it did. That gap, the space between the act and the understanding, is where this sentence plants itself. It doesn't make the wrong smaller. It makes room for the person.
screen: `FATHER: THE FIRST WORD.` · `THE CIRCLE LEFT OPEN.` · `THEY KNOW WHAT, NOT WHAT IT MEANS.` · `ROOM FOR THE PERSON.` · then, large: `FOR THEY KNOW NOT WHAT THEY DO.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle low. Let one person who wronged you come into view. Not to relive it. Just enough to see their face. Then ask a quiet question: what didn't they understand? Maybe what it would cost you. Maybe what was happening in them at the time. Maybe something they still can't see. You don't have to excuse them. Simply wish them one thing: understanding. That someday they see it clearly. If you pray, you can bring them into your prayer with the line from Luke. The bell holds the time.
Father. The first word of Jesus's prayer from the cross in Luke, forgiving the people who didn't know what they were doing. Today's word.
Your line: they know not. Today, when someone hurts or annoys you, ask what they might not see, before you decide what they meant. Day nine hundred fifty.

screen: `DAY 950 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NEITHER DO I CONDEMN THEE.`

951.title: Neither do I condemn thee
951.hook: a woman is brought for stoning, and the crowd leaves one by one (John 8:1–11)
951.howItsDone: Christians read the story of the woman taken in adultery from John 8 as a picture of mercy joined to a call to change.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prayer from the cross. Your line was they know not. Whose blind spot did you try to see? Today, a crowd ready to stone a woman, and a man writing on the ground. Day nine hundred fifty-one.

What should happen to her? That's the question put to Jesus early one morning in the temple, where he's sitting and teaching, with people gathered around. Some scribes and Pharisees, John's Gospel says, bring a woman and set her in the middle. Caught in adultery, they say, in the very act. The law of Moses says such a person should be stoned. What do you say? The text is plain that it's a trap: any answer can be used against him. Everyone is watching. The woman stands there alone. And Jesus doesn't answer. He bends down and starts writing on the ground with his finger. Today: neither do I condemn thee.
screen: `A WOMAN IN THE MIDDLE.` → `A QUESTION THAT'S A TRAP.` → `HE WRITES ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the silence. They keep pressing him, and he keeps writing. John never tells us what he wrote. People have guessed, and the text simply doesn't say. What it does show is a man refusing to be rushed into a verdict. Second, the sentence. Finally he stands up and says, in the King James words: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." Then he bends down and writes again. He doesn't argue the law. He doesn't defend her. He turns the question from her to them, and then looks down again, as if to give them room. Third, the leaving. The text says that those who heard it, "being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, even unto the last." The eldest first. Maybe the ones with the longest memories of their own mistakes. One by one, they go, until only two people are left in that circle. Fourth, the last words. Jesus looks up and asks: "Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee?" She says, "No man, Lord." And he says: "Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." Both halves matter. He doesn't pretend nothing happened; he tells her to go and live differently. But he will not throw the stone, and he sends her out with a future instead of a sentence. Some Christians hear this story as a picture of mercy that is neither cheap nor cruel. The scene ends on a question worth carrying: which stone am I still holding, and what would it take to put it down?
screen: `HE WRITES, AND WAITS.` · `WITHOUT SIN? CAST THE FIRST STONE.` · `ONE BY ONE, THE ELDEST FIRST.` · `NO CONDEMNING, AND A FUTURE.` · then, large: `NEITHER DO I CONDEMN THEE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your hands rest open in your lap. Find one judgment you've been holding about someone. A verdict you've already passed: on a relative, a coworker, someone in the news, maybe yourself. Feel its weight, like a stone in the palm. Now ask the question from the story, gently, with no blame: am I without anything like this myself? Then imagine your fingers loosening, and the stone dropping to the ground. You can still think something was wrong. You're only putting down the throwing. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Accusers. The ones who walked away one by one, until none were left to condemn the woman caught in adultery. Today's word.
Your line: put down the stone. Today, catch one judgment as it forms, about someone in front of you or on a screen, and drop it before you throw it. Day nine hundred fifty-one.

952.title: Zacchaeus gives back
952.hook: a hated tax collector is welcomed, and gives back fourfold (Luke 19:1–10)
952.howItsDone: Christians read the story of Zacchaeus as a picture of welcome leading to repentance and restitution.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crowd that walked away one by one. Your line was put down the stone. Which judgment did you drop? Today, the end of the week, and forgiveness seen from the other side: the one who did the wrong. Day nine hundred fifty-two.

Jericho, and the streets are packed because Jesus is passing through. Somewhere at the back of the crowd is a rich man who can't see a thing. Luke gives us his name, Zacchaeus, his job, chief among the tax collectors, and one more detail: he was little of stature. So he runs ahead and climbs a sycamore tree to watch from the branches. Jesus reaches the spot, stops, looks up, and calls him by name. Today: Zacchaeus gives back.

segments.voice: First, the invitation. In the King James words, Jesus says: "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Not a lecture. Jesus invites himself to the man's house. And Zacchaeus comes down fast and receives him joyfully. Second, the grumbling. Luke says that when people saw it, they all murmured that he had gone to be a guest with a man that is a sinner. The welcome comes first, before any change, and the crowd doesn't like it. Third, the turn. Zacchaeus stands up and says: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Fourfold. Not an apology alone. Not just giving back what he took. Four times over. Nobody demands this of him in the story. It pours out of him once he's been welcomed. Fourth, the answer. Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house," and adds, "the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost." Some readers notice the order here. The welcome came before the repair, and the repair was real and costly. Forgiveness, in this story, doesn't cancel making it right. It sets it free. And that closes the week. We cast crumbs on the water with Tashlich, heard trespasses in the Lord's Prayer, learned from Peter's question, watched the servant forget the talents he'd been forgiven, heard Father, forgive them, and saw a crowd put down its stones. Zacchaeus adds the last piece: the one who has been welcomed gives back more than he took.

segments.voice: Lower your eyes, and let the breath slow. This time, turn the story around. Find one old wrong you did. Something small enough to name, and old enough that it's been quietly sitting there. A loan never repaid. A credit you took. A friend you dropped. Don't punish yourself. Just look at it squarely, the way Zacchaeus named his own dealings. Then ask: what would giving it back look like? Not just even. A little more than even. Let one concrete step come to mind. If you pray, you can hold that step in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
